sections.1:
### Experiment 1. Break on a wrong country feature in the carrier cell, repair by one named component, continue (SAE × mdb watch/edit/continue)

(a) Question. On wrong 3- and 4-hop items the carrier cell (L20 KV6 at the R_argmax row) names a wrong country on 22/27 against 6/83 on correct items (measured, AUDIT-B1). Is that readable error also a *repairable* one at feature grain: can a watch on the cell's SAE country features fire before the answer row is read, and can swapping only the wrong country's feature component for the true country's (a named, minimal edit) restore the answer, without the entity-copy failure that whole-cell donors produce (city-named donors turned the answer into their own city on 15/19, measured, entry 1)?

(b) Pipeline. SAELens supplies the dictionary by registry (`SAE.from_pretrained("qwen-scope-3-1.7b-base-w32k-l50", "layer19")`, strict load, `cfg.metadata` recorded in provenance; mdb's `FeatureBasis.to_saelens()` must agree with it on the active set, as it did 28/28 in TP1) and the country feature list is frozen from entry 1's recurrence table (China f17491, Japan f32521, Greece f22638, Russia f23913, Spain f11201, Netherlands f27085, Italy f26232, plus whatever a cross-item census on the 64 base items adds, with the cross-bridge null ≤ 2/57 as the admission rule; the frozen list is committed before any depth item is opened). mdb: on each of the 154 depth items, `start` with `prefill=@span_first`, `until t<last>.L20.h`; declare `carrier = cache.L20.v[kv6,row=R_argmax]` and its feature bindings by B-a over the L19 basis (the residual at `L20.h` of the carrier row is `L19.h_out`, the SAE's site, measured in entry 1); evaluate the watch `watch feature[COUNTRIES]@carrier edge if best_feature(COUNTRIES) != truth` (B-b). When it fires: `checkpoint wrong`; arm R1 `set carrier += component(truth) - component(best_wrong)` where `component(f) = W_V^g (rho gamma * a_f d_f)` with `a_truth` taken as the median activation of that feature on correct items of the same country (supplied constant, frozen in the prereg) and `a_wrong` the measured activation; arm R2 the whole-cell donor from a correct same-country item (the existing repair, 4/7 and 15/61 measured); arm R3 the error-component swap (E only), as the control that the repair is in the features; `until t<last>.logits`, `verify` against the sealed exact chain, `restart wrong`, next arm. Consumers: M[true language, native wrong answer] and the argmax; co-readout `content(COUNTRIES)` of the repaired cell.

(c) Sealed predictions. W1: the watch fires on ≥ 20/27 wrong d3/d4 items and ≤ 10/83 correct ones (the 22/27 and 6/83 cell readout, now at feature grain; a drop to below 15/27 means the country code is not in the dictionary's country features at this row). W2: R1 moves the argmax to the true language on ≥ 11 of the items where the watch fired, and R1's margin move is ≥ 0.6 of R2's on the median item (the census put 0.82 of the bridge variable in features). W3: R1 produces a donor-entity copy on 0 items, R2 on ≥ 3 of the city-donor items. W4: R3 moves M by less than the floor on ≥ 0.75 of items. Nulls: a random active non-country feature's component swapped at matched norm (expect ≤ 2 repairs); the same R1 edit on correct items (expect ≤ 3/83 argmax changes); the always-last-row cell instead of R_argmax (the B1 null). Falsifier: R1 repairs fewer items than the random-feature null plus 2, or W1 fails; then the readable error is in the cell but not in the dictionary's country features, which is the owner's "SAEs drop variables" at the one site we can test it, and is itself a result.

(d) Cost. Passive part from the 1c captures (K and V at every row are saved): watch evaluation and the whole census, no GPU. Native arms: 27 wrong + 27 matched correct items × (1 fresh run 0.31 s + 4 restored arms 0.10 s) ≈ 40 s of stepping plus about 60 s of model load and about 5 GB host RAM for the single L19 basis; one job under 5 minutes (asserted). A second job if W2 holds: all 154 items with R1 only.

(e) Why both. SAELens has no object that is a KV-cache cell, cannot break on the state of one, cannot edit it and resume the same run, and has no floor; its steering is `h + alpha d` at a residual site. mdb has the cell, the breakpoint, the checkpoint and the verdict, but without the dictionary it cannot say "wrong country", only "wrong content by readout", and it cannot write a *named* minimal correction; its only repair so far is the whole-cell donor, which carries the entity along.
sections.2:
### Experiment 2. SAE features as symbol-table bindings with lifetime and readers at the carrier (SAELens/Qwen-Scope × mdb `symbols`)

(a) Question. Which features carry the country in the L20 KV6 cell, what share of the reader's exact `to_consumer` goes through each feature's component against the error component, and does a feature's lifetime strip (the layers at which it is active at the carrier row) coincide with the cell's causal liveness window (L17 to L21 on the same row, 45/64 items; measured, Run 1 P2 and audit) or with the content strip (country readable from a median of L7; measured, Z1)?

(b) Pipeline. SAELens supplies the L15 to L23 bases by registry (nine layers, about 4.5 GB fp32 host RAM) and their metadata; mdb declares per item `carrier`, `desc` (the rest of the span), `t0`, `relay`, `question` as cell bindings and, by B-a, the top-8 active features at the carrier row as component bindings at each layer 15 to 23, with `Unbound` the error component. `symbols.table(consumer=M[answer, foil], sets=[countries, capitals, entities], content_layers=True)` gives per feature `to_consumer`, `content` of `sum_h W_O,h v_i`, and the partition closure; the lifetime strip is read at two definitions, both reported: (i) the exact projection `<d_f^{(19)}, h_l>` of the fixed L19 direction across layers (exact but a projection), and (ii) the matched-feature lineage by decoder cosine ≥ 0.7 between adjacent layers' SAEs (derived-local). The causal window per item is already measured in Run 1 (`r1-score.json`); the new native arm is `cell_sweep` over layers 15 to 23 at the carrier row with three edits per layer: remove the top country feature's component, remove a random active feature's component at matched norm, remove the error component (B-c supplied vectors into the batched sweep, 27 arms per item, one chunk).

(c) Sealed predictions. L1: the top country feature's component carries ≥ 0.5 of the carrier's `to_consumer` on ≥ 40/64 base items, the error component ≤ 0.2 on ≥ 48/64 (the census 0.82/0.09 at the same cell, now as the exact direct share). L2: the feature-component removal at L20 moves M by ≥ 0.5 of the whole-cell removal on the median item, the random component by ≤ 0.15, the error component by ≤ 0.2. L3: the lifetime strip by lineage first turns on at a median layer ≥ 6 layers before the first causal layer (L18), i.e. features, like content, are readable long before the reader needs them; the falsifier is a lineage onset within 2 layers of L17 on ≥ 40/64, which would make the feature strip the first passive readout that tracks causal liveness. L4: the feature-component removal is above the floor only inside L17 to L21 on ≥ 48/64 items, so the *causal* lifetime of the feature equals the cell's, while its *readable* lifetime does not. Nulls: cross-item (the same feature's component on another item of the family must not name this item's country, expect ≤ 2/60 as in entry 1), shuffled feature id, and the always-last-row cell. Falsifier for the symbol-table claim as a whole: the partition closure fails outside f64 rounding on any item (then B-a is wrong, not the model).

(d) Cost. Table and strips offline from the 1a captures (no GPU; CPU encodes 64 items × 9 layers). Native: 64 items × 27 arms in one `cell_sweep` chunk per item, about 64 × 0.5 s plus load, one job under 3 minutes (asserted from the 0.21 ms per arm anchor).

(e) Why both. Qwen-Scope and SAELens give feature activations at a residual site and nothing about which reader reads them, with what mass, at which layer, or what the reader's exact share of a margin is; they cannot partition a value cell. mdb's table partitions by cell and reports exact shares, but a cell is one row of the table with no names inside it; the feature component is the first sub-cell binding, and the partition check is the first exactness test an SAE decomposition has had against a causal unit.
sections.3:
### Experiment 3. Where hop 3 is made: transcoder features nominate answer-row MLP writers, mdb's ladder measures them (circuit-tracer transcoders × mdb `hop_edge`)

(a) Question. The language (hop 3) is not shown to be in the carrier cell (75/132 with the country direction projected out, AUDITED unknown) and mean-ablating the answer row's MLPs at L_c to L_c+2 costs the language margin less than the capital margin on all six models (B6, AUDITED inverted). Do the Qwen3-1.7B transcoders name recurring MLP features at the answer row, L20 to L25, that write the language, and does removing their writes natively drop the language margin more than the capital margin?

(b) Pipeline. Transcoders read `L.n` (after the norm gain, measured in entry 5) and write `L.m`; encode on CPU from the 1c captures (`n` at L ≥ 20 is saved for the answer row), layers 20 to 25 (six files, about 8 GB bf16 host RAM), on the 105 correct d2 to d4 items and the 27 wrong ones. Nomination rule, frozen: per layer the features whose decoder direction has direct effect `rho^F c_lang . a_s d_s ≥ 0.25` on M[language, runner-up language] and that recur on ≥ 3 items of the same language with a cross-language null ≤ 1/50 of other items; keep the top 5 per item. mdb: for each item, `checkpoint` at `t<last>.L20.m`; arms per nominated feature `set L<l>.m += -a_s d_s` (B-c supplied, the transcoder's own activation and direction, with the transcoder error left in place), the joint top-5 removal, a matched-norm random active transcoder feature, and the existing mean ablation of the whole MLP at the same layer; `hop_edge(..., neurons=True)` splits each arm's effect into direct, later-MLP, re-read, norm and rounding and names the SwiGLU neurons that realise the feature's write; consumers M[language, runner-up language] and M[capital, runner-up capital] read in the same arm; `verify` against the sealed exact chain.

(c) Sealed predictions. H1: at least 3 recurring language-writing features exist in L21 to L24 with cross-language null ≤ 1/50 (the SAE recurrence at the carrier was 7/7 vs 1/57 for China; the MLP side should recur too if hop 3 is a lookup there). H2: the joint top-5 removal drops the language margin by ≥ 2× the capital margin on the median correct depth item, which is the B6 prediction restated at feature grain. H3: the random-feature arm is within the floor on ≥ 0.75 of items. H4: on wrong items whose carrier names the *true* country (the 5/27 non-readable errors), the nominated features' activations are below the correct-item median on ≥ 4/5, which would locate those errors at hop 3. Falsifier: H2 fails with H1 holding, i.e. recurring language features exist but their native removal moves capital as much as language; then hop 3 is not realised by these MLP writes at the answer row and the remaining candidates are the cell (experiment 2's co-readout) or L26 to L27, which the Base-unfit L26 transcoder cannot name. The transcoder's error term is reported as its own row with the direct share, never folded.

(d) Cost. Encodes offline on CPU (132 items × 6 layers × one 32K-wide matvec, seconds). Native: 132 items × (fresh run 0.31 s + 8 restored arms × 0.10 s) ≈ 2.5 min plus load; the `hop_edge` neuron ladder at 1.7B ran 64 items in 3:35 (Z2, measured), so one job of about 8 minutes, or two jobs if the ladder is kept at `neurons=True` for all arms.

(e) Why both. The transcoder set names MLP features and their decoder writes but has no native intervention on Base, no co-consumer accounting and no floor; circuit-tracer's graphs would freeze attention and norms and report edges on the post-trained model. mdb's `hop_edge` gives the exact per-layer and per-neuron split and the native arm, but it names neurons by index and cannot say which of 6,144 neurons at a layer form "the language writer" across items; the transcoder feature is the name that recurs.
sections.4:
### Experiment 4. The attribution-graph gap, split into brackets with floors (circuit-tracer edges via nnsight gradients × mdb frozen-pattern arms)

(a) Question. Entry 5 measured that transcoder direct edges overstate native effects about 2× (median native/edge 0.53; Spearman 0.92; 7/18 nodes below the floor). Which part of the gap is attention re-routing, which part is the norm-scale freeze, and which part is MLP nonlinearity and feature switching, per node, with a floor on each bracket? The hop-2 ladder's re-read share was −0.01 median at 1.7B (Z2, measured), so the standing objection to attribution graphs, frozen attention, is predicted to be the *smallest* bracket at the pending row.

(b) Pipeline. nnsight `grads` (one forward and one backward per batch of same-length prompts) supplies the graph edge `A_{s→M}` of each nominated transcoder node at the answer row: the gradient of M with respect to `L.m` with the attention probabilities and the RMSNorm scales detached inside the eager attention and norm ops (via `.source` access on the weight-sharing clone; asserted feasible, and if it is not, run circuit-tracer in its own transformers-4.57 environment and import the graph JSON, which is the tracker's stated next step). mdb seals, per node, three numbers before any arm: `-A_{s→M}` (supplied), its own linear term with the true Jacobian (derived-local) and the exact float64 chain. Four native arms per node from one checkpoint at `t<last>.L<l>.m`: arm 0 free (`set L<l>.m += -a_s d_s`); arm 1 the same with `p` at layers l+1 to 27 of the answer row replaced by the base run's `p` (P-port edits at each later layer stop, the edit value read from the base checkpoint); arm 2 arm 1 plus the norm scales held at base (`set L<l'>.a = gamma * h * rho_base` and the same for `n` at each later stop; a dependent edit realised by reading `h` at the stop and writing `a`, which the Python API allows); arm 3 is the sealed linear edge itself. Brackets, each a difference of two measured numbers: re-routing = arm 0 − arm 1; norm scale = arm 1 − arm 2; nonlinearity plus feature switching = arm 2 − (−A); rounding = mdb's residual. The transcoder-error bracket (real later MLPs against transcoders under identical freezes) needs the replacement model's forward and is deferred: with the 1.7B set at 1.34 GB per layer it does not fit beside the model on 16 GB and is a CPU job on its own.

(c) Sealed predictions. G1: the re-routing bracket has median magnitude ≤ 0.1 of |arm 0| over node-items (from the −0.01 re-read share). G2: the nonlinearity bracket is the largest of the three on ≥ 0.6 of node-items and explains the 2× overstatement (median (arm 2 − (−A)) / (arm 0 − (−A)) ≥ 0.5). G3: the norm-scale bracket is below the floor on ≥ 0.7 of node-items. G4: Spearman between −A and arm 0 stays ≥ 0.85 (entry 5 gave 0.92 on 18 nodes). Nulls: the same four arms for a matched-norm random active feature (all brackets within floor on ≥ 0.75), and the per-arm `null_vs_stepped` check that the frozen-p and frozen-scale machinery alone, with no feature edit, reproduces the base margin within 2 spacings (if it does not, the arms are not clean and the job stops). Falsifier: G1 fails with the re-routing bracket ≥ 0.3 of |arm 0| on the median node; then frozen attention *is* the dominant error of attribution graphs on this model at the pending row, which is the headline the field would want and which contradicts the hop-2 ladder.

(d) Cost. 32 base items (the prompts entry 5 used plus the 1a items of the same four families) × top-5 nodes × 3 native arms = 480 stepped arms; the frozen arms step every later layer with a port edit, so about 0.5 s each (asserted from the 0.31 s fresh-run anchor plus 7 to 8 extra stops), about 4 minutes plus the nnsight batch (seconds) and load: one job of about 6 minutes. Transcoder encodes on CPU for L20 to L24 only (the Base-fit layers).

(e) Why both. circuit-tracer can freeze patterns and scales inside its replacement model, but every edge it reports is a linear estimate on the post-trained model with no floor and no native arm; nnsight gives the gradient under the freezes in one batch but has no notion of a sealed prediction, an exact chain or a rounding residual. mdb cannot nominate feature nodes and has no graph, but it is the only one of the three that can realise "attention frozen, everything else native" as an actual run and report each bracket against a measured floor.
sections.5:
### Experiment 5. Out-of-sample composer neurons: an nnsight attribution-patching forecast sealed in mdb and verified natively at scale (nnsight `grads` + `batch_whatif` × mdb `forecast`/`verify`)

(a) Question. The named L20 to L27 neurons beat a random and an answer-token null on 32/34 items, but they were selected on the same items (AUDIT-RUN1: selection on outcome remains). Can a gradient-times-activation forecast of neuron ablation effects (attribution patching, the field's cheap estimator) be sealed on one half of the panel and verified on the other half with a floor, and how much of its known 2× underestimate is per-layer and predictable?

(b) Pipeline. nnsight `grads` over the 64 base items gives `dM/df` at `L<l>.f` for l = 20 to 27 in one forward and backward per length group (96 prompts took 10 s in TP1); the forecast per neuron is `-(dM/df) · f`. Split by country: panel A (32 items) nominates per country the top 8 neurons per layer by summed forecast, with the recurrence rule and the answer-token-fixed null from the Run 1 audit; panel B (32 items) is held out. mdb seals, per panel-B item, the forecast record for every nominated neuron and for the named set (supplied, with the nnsight version and the address map), then measures natively: nnsight `batch_whatif` runs the 64 single-neuron ablations plus the set, the random set and the answer-token-null set per item as one batch (14 arms took 0.56 s on 1.5B; here about 70 arms per item, asserted 2 to 3 s), and mdb `verify` re-measures 2 arms per item stepped (5 to 6 s each, I4) with the kernel-path delta `batched − stepped` recorded as part of the floor (the T2 precedent: edited arms differed from stepped by up to 0.625, so the floor must carry it).

(c) Sealed predictions. N1: the out-of-sample named set moves M by ≥ 0.5 more than the random set on ≥ 24/32 panel-B items and beats the answer-token null on ≥ 22/32 (in-sample was 33/34 and 32/34). N2: Spearman between the forecast and the native single-neuron effect over neurons with |native| > floor is ≥ 0.8; the size ratio forecast/native is 0.4 to 0.7 (Run 1: 0.28 to 0.73 for cells, nonlinearity inside SwiGLU). N3: the per-layer ratio rises with depth, L20 ≤ 0.5 and L26 to L27 ≥ 0.8 (Run 0 gave 0.41 at L20 and 0.79 to 0.95 at L25 to L27 for cell edits), so the miss is where SwiGLU sees a large input change, not at the readout. N4: `batched − stepped` is within 2 spacings on ≥ 0.9 of verified arms; if not, the floor absorbs it and the verdicts are re-stated. Falsifier: N1 fails; then the composer neurons are item-specific and "named neurons" was a selection artefact, which closes the P8 caveat negatively.

(d) Cost. One job: nnsight gradients (10 to 20 s), batched arms 32 × 3 s, 64 stepped verifications × 6 s ≈ 6.5 min, load 1 min; about 9 minutes, so split the verification into a second job if the first smoke runs over 7 minutes.

(e) Why both. nnsight gives gradients and batched arms at a rate mdb cannot (one stepped `whatif` is 1.3 to 13.5 s), but it has no forecast record, no floor, no exact chain and no account of the batched-versus-stepped kernel difference; without mdb its number is a measurement with no verdict. mdb has the sealed forecast, the floor and the stepped authority but cannot differentiate (its linear term is a forward-mode Jacobian at one address, not a gradient over 6,144 neurons at eight layers) and cannot batch.
sections.6:
### Experiment 6. TransformerLens weight processing as a reparametrisation null: how much of a patching verdict is rounding (TL 4.4 bridge × mdb floor)

(a) Question. `enable_compatibility_mode()` folds the norm gains and centres the unembedding on RMSNorm models (verified in source, library review). Both are exact reparametrisations: margins are invariant to a per-position logit constant and `fold_ln` changes no function. So in exact arithmetic every patching effect on the processed bridge equals the native one, and the measured difference is a realisation of bf16 rounding under a different operation order. Does mdb's floor (2 bf16 spacings at the result's magnitude, M51) cover that realised distribution, and how many published-style head-patching verdicts flip under reparametrisation alone? This is tracker entry 7 (bf16 noise-floor meta-study) made concrete. The one prior data point is suspicious: on Qwen2.5-0.5B the margin moved +0.125 and attention weights moved by up to 0.46 (entry 5, job-1ea14f38c875); 0.46 is about a hundred bf16 spacings of a probability near 0.5, so either the processing is not a pure reparametrisation on Qwen2 (QKV biases, or a bias fold) or something in the bridge differs; the fp32 leg below separates the two.

(b) Pipeline. Models Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B-Base (both fit the bridge; 1.5B went out of memory, I5), the 48 base-family items of the scale panel per model, consumers M[answer, foil]. TL: an unprocessed bridge (bitwise equal to mdb's trace, measured 560/560 hooks on 1.7B) and a processed bridge on a separate clone, each run in bf16 on GPU and in fp32 on CPU; `run_with_cache` with `names_filter` from `names.to_tl`; TL's own `logit_attrs` and head-zeroing patches at the carrier layer's query heads and the carrier V cell interchange (sequence scope, as entry 5 did). mdb: the same edits natively (`cell_sweep` for the cell, `whatif` for the heads) with floors; `tl.processing()` recorded in provenance; the processed values are *not* imported into mdb (the refusal stands); instead TL's processed numbers enter as `supplied` claims through `interop.verify`, and mdb scores each claim's agreement with native against its floor.

(c) Sealed predictions. R1 (fp32 leg): processed and unprocessed margins agree within 1e-4 on 48/48 items per model; any larger gap means the processing is not a pure reparametrisation on that family (then report which tensor differs; QKV bias folding on Qwen2.5 is my guess, asserted). R2 (bf16 leg): |processed − native| on the margin is within mdb's floor on ≥ 0.9 of items and on ≥ 0.9 of the 48 × 20 patch effects; the distribution's 95th percentile is reported as the measured floor and compared with the 2-spacing rule. R3: among patch effects that mdb's verdict calls "effect" (above floor), ≤ 5% change sign or fall below floor on the processed bridge; among effects below floor, ≥ 30% change sign, so a verdict is stable exactly when the floor says it is. R4: attention-weight changes ≥ 0.1 occur on 0 items in fp32; if they recur in bf16 only, they are a softmax amplification of rounding at near-tied keys and the affected heads are listed. Nulls: unprocessed bridge against mdb (must be bitwise, the known parity), and two unprocessed bf16 forwards with different batch composition (the kernel-path delta, T2), which bounds how much of R2 is the processing and how much is any reordering. Falsifier for the memo's claim that the 2-spacing floor is right: the 95th percentile of the reparametrisation difference exceeds 4 spacings on either model.

(d) Cost. CPU fp32 legs for 0.5B and 0.6B are minutes each (48 items, two bridges); the bf16 legs on GPU are seconds; mdb native arms 48 × 20 via `cell_sweep` and 48 × 4 `whatif`s per model about 3 minutes. Two jobs, one per model, each under 8 minutes (asserted); the processed bridge of 0.6B in fp32 needs about 6 GB of RAM (asserted from 23.7 GB at 1.7B).

(e) Why both. TransformerLens produces the reparametrised computation and the patching utilities the community uses, but it has no floor and cannot say whether a changed verdict is rounding or model; mdb has the floor and the native authority but cannot produce a mathematically equivalent alternative realisation of the same forward, which is what makes the rounding distribution measurable instead of asserted.
sections.7:
### Experiment 7. Interchange intervention accuracy at the carrier cell, with a floor and a training-free subspace (pyvene × mdb branches × SAE pushforward)

(a) Question. In the field's own metric, what is the interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) of the carrier V cell across entity pairs, how many dimensions of the 128-dim cell carry the country, and is that subspace the pushforward of the Qwen-Scope country features (a subspace obtained with no training) rather than a trained DAS rotation?

(b) Pipeline. pyvene (pip, Apache-2.0; not installed on Beast; Qwen3 component names must be checked against its source first, asserted) expresses the intervention as a shareable config: vanilla interchange on `value_output` at layer 20, position R_argmax, restricted to the KV6 slice, source = the donor item; mdb runs the identical edit as `set cache.L20.v[kv6,row] = @donor:cache.L20.v[kv6,row]` and the two must agree within one bf16 step on every pair (the survey's parity proof; entry 5's three-tool Eiffel numbers differed by up to 0.3 between TL sequence scope and mdb reader scope, so scope must be matched to the cell, not the position). Three interchange variants per pair, all as mdb branches from one checkpoint: whole cell; the subspace `Pi_SAE` = orthonormal basis of `{W_V^g (rho gamma d_f) : f in the frozen country feature list active in either run}` (rank reported, expected ≤ 12); a random subspace of the same rank. Optional comparator, run only if the owner approves training: pyvene DAS at ranks 4, 8, 16 trained on 24 pairs and tested on the other 24, with cos(range(Pi_DAS), range(Pi_SAE)) reported. IIA counts a flip only when the post-edit margin's sign change exceeds mdb's floor; each branch's exact chain and nonlinear share are recorded.

(c) Sealed predictions. I1: whole-cell IIA on the 123 different-bridge pairs of entry 1 is 0.55 to 0.65 (71/123 flips measured, now with the floor). I2: the SAE-pushforward subspace reaches ≥ 0.8 of whole-cell IIA at rank ≤ 12; the random subspace ≤ 0.2 of it. I3: the pyvene and mdb whole-cell margins agree within one bf16 step on 123/123 pairs. I4 (if DAS is run): rank-8 DAS IIA exceeds the pushforward's by ≤ 0.1, and cos between the two ranges is ≥ 0.6 on the median pair; if DAS beats the pushforward by ≥ 0.2, the trained subspace carries country content the dictionary's features do not span, which is the owner's hypothesis in subspace form. Nulls: same-bridge controls (expect the 47/53 to 52/63 rate of entry 1, with the city-donor failures listed), and the K cell (expect 0/123). Falsifier for I2: the pushforward subspace is below 0.5 of whole-cell IIA; then the country variable in the cell is not spanned by the residual SAE's country features even though the census said the features carry 0.82 of the effect, and the difference would be between "features at the residual" and "their image in the cell", which experiment 2's component bindings would then have to explain.

(d) Cost. 123 pairs × 4 branches by `cell_sweep` (supplied vectors), seconds; pyvene parity on 123 pairs at batch 1, about 0.3 s each, under a minute; DAS training, if approved, seconds on 128-dim cells. One job under 5 minutes.

(e) Why both. pyvene gives the declarative config other labs can rerun and the IIA metric they accept, and DAS if wanted; it has no floor, so a flip inside two spacings counts, and it has no cell-level site, only a position and a component. mdb has the cell, the floor and the exact chain but no shared intervention format and no accepted abstraction metric; the SAE supplies the only training-free candidate subspace, which neither pyvene nor mdb could name.
